meta.title: F1 numbers and cards: the five scales of an energy system
meta.lessons: Per scale, the lessons that go further, by starter number or code: LX.ScaleStrip links a lesson when data/path.json marks it live, and names it as upcoming (with its note) otherwise.
meta.note: The scale definitions follow the course's definition of a scale (decisions, authority, physics, inputs, outputs). The scales are overlapping views, not levels of authority: a city and a grid region can share land, and one organisation can act at two scales. Prairie Town, Prairie Campus, the Plains Grid, Prairie City and Prairieland are fictional; their sizes are illustrative. The real anchors (electricity bought per U.S. residential customer, as average power; the Southwest Power Pool's 2025 peak; the Lower 48 record hour) are read from 01-power-energy.json and town_days.json, where each carries its source and date. Prairie Town's 450 MW is the highest hour of its illustrative year (SPP's 2025 demand shape scaled so that SPP's highest hour is 450 MW: town.json and town_year.json), not the peak of lesson 0's day.
meta.gloss: Each scale's `gloss` is one line under the zoom's caption that defines the scene's terms at first use (glossary marks).

scales.name: Device and plant
scales.setting: A Prairie Town home, and the wind farm on the ridge
scales.question: What should one site install, and how should it run hour by hour?
scales.who: The owner of the home or plant, within tariffs, codes and connection rules
scales.what: What to install at one site, and how to run it hour by hour
scales.physics: Device ratings, efficiencies, a battery's state of charge, one meter
scales.inputs: Tariffs or prices, weather, connection limits from the host grid
scales.outputs: A load or supply profile, and flexibility at the meter

scales.name: Microgrid and community
scales.setting: Prairie Campus: a college, the county hospital and a rural co-op
scales.gloss: A [[microgrid|microgrid]] can [[islanding|island]]: disconnect from the grid and keep its own loads running. It links to the grid through a [[feeder|feeder]], a local power line.
scales.question: How do we keep critical services running in an outage, and who owns the system?
scales.who: A campus owner or a rural co-op, under the utility's connection and tariff rules
scales.what: How big to build, which loads stay on when it islands, who owns it, local trading
scales.physics: A campus or feeder network that can island, within safe voltage limits
scales.inputs: The tariff, the host feeder's export and import limits, outage statistics
scales.outputs: Net load, offers of flexibility, resilience of critical services

scales.name: Regional bulk grid
scales.setting: The Plains Grid: three zones, with Prairie Town one node in the west
scales.gloss: A [[synchronous-grid|synchronous grid]] shares one AC [[frequency|frequency]]. Synchronous generators rotate in step electrically; [[inverter|inverters]] connect other resources to that frequency; several operators can share the grid, each balancing its own region.
scales.question: Will there be enough power, what sets prices, and how should a large new load connect?
scales.who: A grid operator (a regional market operator or a utility, acting as balancing authority), overseen by regulators
scales.what: Which plants run in its region, reserves, new transmission, capacity and connections
scales.physics: Power flow on lines; frequency and inertia when a study looks at fast disturbances
scales.inputs: Aggregated loads and small resources, fuel prices, policy, power traded with neighbouring regions
scales.outputs: Prices, reliability, emission factors, connection timelines

scales.name: City and region
scales.setting: Prairie City (about 250,000 people), its farms, an industrial park and a new data-center campus (a large load)
scales.gloss: A city's [[building-code|building codes]] and land rules shape its demand; the grid region that overlaps the same land is run by someone else.
scales.question: How should a city save, heat, cool, move and power itself, fairly?
scales.who: A city or county (often building codes, land, transit), with utilities and owners; running the regional grid is a different role
scales.what: Buildings, heat, transport, land use, local supply, distribution upgrades
scales.physics: Distribution feeders, heat networks, coupling across buildings, transport and power
scales.inputs: Grid prices and emission factors, state and national policy
scales.outputs: Demand trajectories, local siting, distribution needs

scales.name: Nation
scales.setting: Prairieland: five regions, one strait for oil imports, coal-dependent Ridge County
scales.gloss: A national energy balance adds up every fuel that enters and leaves each region, from imported oil to electricity.
scales.question: Which pathway keeps a nation secure, affordable, clean and fair?
scales.who: A national government and its regulators
scales.what: Targets, instruments, infrastructure, emergency stocks, trade
scales.physics: Energy balances for each region (primary and final), the main power lines between regions
scales.inputs: World prices, technology availability, climate commitments
scales.outputs: Policy and price signals, targets and budgets passed down to regions

predict.q: A heat wave is pushing demand toward a record. Who decides which power plants run in the next hour?

cards.text: A homeowner, or a plant's owner, within the tariff and building codes
cards.why: One owner decides for one site: what to install behind one meter and how to run it, under the utility's [[tariff|tariff]].

cards.text: A campus owner or a rural co-op, under the utility's rules
cards.why: A microgrid's owner sizes it and sets its priorities, but the host utility sets the rules at the connection.

cards.text: A grid operator (a regional market operator or a utility), overseen by regulators
cards.why: A regional operator, a [[balancing-authority|balancing authority]], runs plants so that supply equals demand in its region at every moment.

cards.text: A city or county: building codes (rules for new buildings), land, transit
cards.why: City planning often shapes buildings, land and transport. Running the regional grid is a different role, even when a city owns a utility.

cards.text: A national government and its regulators
cards.why: A nation sets targets, instruments, national infrastructure and trade.

cards.text: What to install at one site, and how to run it hour by hour
cards.why: Rooftop solar, a heat pump or a battery, and their hourly schedule, are one site's choices.

cards.text: How big to build, and which loads stay on when it runs alone
cards.why: Sizing and load priorities in an outage are the microgrid's own decisions.

cards.text: Which plants run each hour and the reserves; a say in new lines and connections
cards.why: An operator schedules plants and reserves for its own region; planners, utilities and regulators share decisions about new lines and connections.

cards.text: Building codes, heat networks, transit, where solar may go, feeder upgrades
cards.why: These shape a city's demand and local supply over years.

cards.text: Targets, taxes and standards, emergency fuel stocks, trade
cards.why: National instruments set the signals every smaller scale works within.

physics.title: What these example models focus on

cards.text: Device ratings, efficiencies, a battery's state of charge, one meter
cards.why: A home scheduling model usually represents the devices and treats the grid connection as a limit.

cards.text: A small network that can disconnect and run alone, within safe voltage limits
cards.why: Islanding is what makes a microgrid; its model usually checks that the island can keep its loads supplied.

cards.text: Power flow on lines; frequency and inertia for fast disturbances
cards.why: A regional grid's lines limit what can flow where; studies of sudden events also track its [[frequency|frequency]] and [[inertia|inertia]].

cards.text: Distribution feeders, heat networks, links between buildings, transport and power
cards.why: A city model couples sectors: heat, transport and power share streets and feeders.

cards.text: Energy balances for each region, the main power lines between regions
cards.why: A national model usually keeps regions and fuels in balance and leaves out individual feeders.

bins.label: Passed down
bins.sub: a signal or a limit sent to a smaller scale

bins.label: Passed up
bins.sub: a profile or a need sent to a larger scale

cards.text: Utility → household: a tariff
cards.why: Here the utility sets the price; the home's schedule takes it as given.

cards.text: Grid operator → campus: an export limit
cards.why: The host grid tells a campus or a plant how much it may export or import.

cards.text: Nation → regions and cities: targets and budgets
cards.why: A nation passes targets and budgets down to its regions and cities.

cards.text: Household → grid operator: an hourly load and its flexibility
cards.why: Millions of homes' profiles add up to the demand a grid operator plans for.

cards.text: Campus → host utility: its net load and outage needs
cards.why: A microgrid shows the grid only its net load and what flexibility it offers.

cards.text: City → regional planners: a demand forecast and where it wants new solar
cards.why: City plans feed regional and national planning.

cards.text: Will it cut my bill under my tariff, and keep the fridge on in an outage?
cards.why: A household weighs its own bill and its own outages.

cards.text: Can it keep the hospital running after the campus disconnects, until its generator starts?
cards.why: A microgrid asks about its critical loads when it runs on its own.

cards.text: Does it lower the cost of the evening peak and supply reserves?
cards.why: A grid operator values batteries for the whole system's peak and reserves.

cards.text: Where would batteries put off a feeder upgrade, and which neighborhoods gain?
cards.why: A city asks where, and who benefits.

cards.text: How much storage does the national pathway need, and what does it mean for imports?
cards.why: A nation asks about totals, pathways and security.

apply.q: Prairie Campus planned its cheapest [[microgrid|microgrid]] assuming it could export all its midday solar, but the host [[feeder|feeder]] now sets an export limit below what that plan sends out at noon. What must happen?

options.label: Nothing: the old plan still stands
Recheck the plan: its operation must change, and the cheapest equipment may change too

feedback.same: The old schedule breaks the new limit, so it is no longer allowed: the campus's best plan holds only within the limits it was given.
feedback.changes: At least the schedule must change: store or spill some solar. Whether the cheapest equipment changes too takes a new run of the campus model.
feedback.none: Plans that export less still work: the campus can store, spill or build less. The plan changes; it does not vanish.

optimum: The cheapest plan for one campus may not be the cheapest for everyone connected to the grid. A limit from another scale, like a feeder's export cap, can change the campus's best plan.
